article.headline: Quant Funds Load Up on Apple, Nvidia, and Linde in Q1 2026
article.lede: Fresh 13F filings — the quarterly SEC disclosures that reveal what large institutional managers held at each quarter's end — show systematic funds adding heavily to Apple (AAPL), Nvidia (NVDA), and Linde (LIN) during the first three months of 2026. The data became available as the May 15 filing deadline passed, offering the first aggregated read on where algorithmic money moved during a quarter dominated by tariff shocks and AI-infrastructure spending. The figures come from @InTheAssembly, a financial commentary account that aggregates 13F data.
article.body:
Apple (AAPL) had the roughest start to 2026 of any mega-cap. In early April the company shed an estimated $638 billion in market value as tariff escalation — duties as high as 145% on Chinese imports — threatened both its manufacturing supply chain and its second-largest consumer market. The reversal came fast: a 90-day tariff pause announced around May 7 relit investor confidence, and Apple's fiscal second-quarter earnings, reported April 30, were emphatic. Revenue reached $111.2 billion (up 17% year-over-year), earnings per share hit $2.01 (up 22%), and Greater China revenue surged 28%. The board added a $100 billion buyback authorization, and the stock hit a new all-time closing high of $300.23 on May 15. That sequence — sharp drawdown followed by earnings blowout and buyback — is precisely what quant *momentum* and *earnings-revision* models are designed to identify, explaining the $781 million net add.

Nvidia (NVDA) requires less narrative. Its position as the dominant supplier of *GPUs* (graphics processing units, the specialized chips central to AI model training) has been the defining equity story of the past three years, and the institutional bid has not relented. Analysts expect the company to report roughly $78.8 billion in revenue for its fiscal first quarter on May 20 — continued explosive growth. Renaissance Technologies, the quantitative firm whose Medallion Fund is the closest thing finance has to a perpetual-motion machine, reportedly increased its Nvidia stake by 190% in Q1 2026, a striking move from the canonical quant shop. Arrowstreet Capital, another systematic manager, raised its $5.54 billion Nvidia position by a further 19%.

The most instructive name is **Linde** (LIN). As the world's largest industrial gases company by revenue — roughly $34 billion in 2025 — Linde occupies an unglamorous but structurally durable corner of the economy: it produces and distributes oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, and specialty gases to steel mills, hospitals, semiconductor fabs, and data centers under long-term, *take-or-pay* contracts. Those contracts — often 15 to 20 years, with supply infrastructure built adjacent to the customer's site — create switching costs so high that churn is nearly nonexistent. That formula has made Linde the archetypal *compounder*: a company that generates high returns on invested capital and can redeploy them at similarly high rates, compounding intrinsic value decade after decade.

Linde (LIN) spent 2024 and much of 2025 underperforming the broader market by a wide margin as European industrial activity slowed, energy prices swung unpredictably (energy is 30–40% of production cost), and the clean-hydrogen buildout moved slower than expected. The recovery narrative has three threads. First, semiconductor fab demand: Linde supplies the specialty gases that chip manufacturers cannot operate without, and its electronics-segment revenue — roughly $4 billion today — is growing at double-digit rates on the back of AI infrastructure investment. Second, a hydrogen pipeline: management expects $2.5–$3 billion in hydrogen-related projects to begin generating revenue in 2026. Third, a clean Q1 2026 earnings beat — $4.33 adjusted earnings per share against a $4.27 consensus — with full-year guidance raised. That combination of quality-factor credentials and fresh earnings momentum is what brings a compounder back.

concepts.definition: A quarterly SEC disclosure form required of any U.S. institutional investment manager overseeing $100 million or more in domestic equity assets. It must be filed within 45 days of each quarter's end and lists all long equity positions — the primary public window into large-fund stock ownership, though it is backward-looking and reveals only what was held, not why.

An investment fund that makes buy and sell decisions using mathematical models, statistical algorithms, and machine learning rather than human judgment. Quant funds screen for systematic signals — momentum, earnings revisions, buyback yield, quality factors — across hundreds or thousands of stocks simultaneously and rebalance mechanically when those signals shift.

A company that generates high returns on invested capital and can reinvest those returns at similarly high rates year after year, causing intrinsic value to grow exponentially over time. Classic compounders have durable competitive moats — pricing power, switching costs, or a structural supply position — that protect their economics across economic cycles.

A long-term supply agreement in which the buyer commits to pay for a minimum volume of a commodity or service whether or not they actually take delivery. For Linde, these contracts — typically 15–20 years, with supply infrastructure built adjacent to the customer's facility — provide highly predictable recurring revenue and make switching to a competitor economically prohibitive.

A quantitative factor measuring the direction and magnitude of changes in analyst earnings estimates. When estimates are revised upward repeatedly, quant models treat it as a signal of improving fundamentals and increase portfolio weighting in the affected stock.

Graphics processing unit — a chip originally designed to render images whose massively parallel architecture makes it ideal for the matrix mathematics at the core of deep-learning model training. Nvidia is the dominant GPU supplier for AI workloads.

ticker_aapl.name: Apple Inc.
ticker_aapl.blurb: Apple designs and markets consumer electronics (iPhone, Mac, iPad, Apple Watch), software, and digital services. The iPhone remains the dominant revenue driver, but the Services segment — comprising the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud, Apple Pay, and licensing — has grown into a high-margin business that Wall Street values separately. Apple commands one of the highest brand loyalty rates in consumer technology and operates a tightly integrated hardware-software ecosystem.
ticker_aapl.recent: Apple reported FY2025 revenue of approximately $400 billion. The company has faced headwinds from slowing iPhone upgrade cycles in mature markets and regulatory pressure on App Store commissions in both the US and EU. Apple Intelligence, its generative AI suite, launched in late 2024 but has not yet materially re-accelerated upgrade cycles. Paul Pelosi sold 45,000 shares of AAPL according to the January 2026 PTR disclosure — the largest single sale in the filing by share count.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_lin.name: Linde plc
ticker_lin.blurb: Linde plc is a global industrial gas company that supplies atmospheric gases (oxygen, nitrogen, argon, rare gases) and process gases (hydrogen, helium, carbon dioxide, electronic gases, specialty gases, acetylene). It also designs and constructs turnkey process plants for third-party customers, including air separation, hydrogen, synthesis, olefin, and natural gas plants. Serving healthcare, chemicals, energy, and other industries, Linde is one of the largest industrial gas companies in the world, with a market capitalization of approximately $234 billion and over 65,000 employees.
ticker_lin.recent: As of May 15, 2026, Linde's stock price was $506.11, down 1.08% on the day, with a 52-week range of $387.78 to $521.28. The company reported earnings on May 1, 2026, and has a forward P/E of 27.69. Analysts rate the stock a Strong Buy with a price target of $546.63, representing an 8.01% upside.
